newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian rebels hold hostages for third night.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian rebels hold hostages for third night.

text.p: The lives of nearly 400 men held captive in the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima for three days remained in the balance on Friday with no sign of an early solution to the standoff between leftist guerrillas and Peru's government.

Still clad in elegant clothes for the cocktail party that the rebels stormed on Tuesday, the men spent another uncomfortable night on the floor, made do with meagre food and water supplies and lined up to use the residence's four toilets.

The hostages -- high-ranking diplomats, foreign businessmen and top government officials -- were believed to be one of the largest and most valuable human hauls ever held by a guerrilla group, experts said.

In the street outside, dozens of Peruvians held a candle- lit vigil through the night. Nearby residents put out Peruvian flags and hundreds of police, family members and journalists played a tense waiting game with the approximately 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) guerrillas inside.

"There are 24 million Peruvians who will not allow the lives of those kidnapped to be threatened. We condemn this kidnapping but at the same time look for a solution," said one of the vigil organisers, legislator Manuel Lajo.
Tentative negotiations with the rebels have produced no apparent progress although four dazed hostages, one in a wheelchair, were released late on Thursday.

Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, facing one of the most serious crises of his political career, promised in a letter to U.S. President Bill Clinton that the safety of hostages would be his first priority in resolving the siege.

"I want to assure your excellency that I am occupying myself permanently and jointly with my team to achieve a solution as soon as possible to this crisis, the principal objective being the safeguarding of the health and life of those who are inside," he wrote in the letter.
Fujimori, who ignored an ultimatum by the rebels for his presence on Wednesday, has still not made a public statement since the crisis began.

On Thursday night, he held a one-hour emergency meeting with Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda, who arrived earlier in the day to help negotiate the crisis. The pair emerged stony-faced from the meeting at Government Palace in downtown Lima, but gave no comments.

The shocking attack posed a tough dilemma for Fujimori as he juggled his domestically popular tough stance against guerrillas with competing political, economic and international pressures. As the embassy residence is legally on Japanese territory, Fujimori would in theory need Tokyo's approval for any assault.
The rebels have threatened to kill their captives if Peru does not release up to 500 of their imprisoned comrades.
Details of conditions inside the residence were scant.

Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent, released late Tuesday with three other diplomats to mediate between rebels and the government, said conditions in the residence, normally home to six people, were very cramped. "They're packed in," he said.
Red Cross official Juan Pedro Schaerer, however, said: "The hostages are well. Nobody is sick." He added that rebels had given the hostages permission to write letters to relatives.

The Red Cross supplied the captives with water, some food, medical supplies and even chess sets and rosary chains. The organisation said 380 hostages were left inside after about 100 women and elderly were freed at the start of the crisis.
Governments worldwide have urged Peru not to use force and to do everything in its power to protect the hostages.

The United States on Thursday sent a team of security advisers to Lima to assist the U.S. ambassador to Peru in the crisis, the State Department said. The ambassador and his deputy attended the reception, but left before the siege began.

The rebels assaulted the fortified compound from outside on Tuesday, linking up with comrades disguised as waiters inside a cocktail reception to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday, anti-terrorist police sources said. Cartridges were smuggled into the building beforehand among flowers and inside a Christmas cake.

The rebels released Fujimori's mother and sister, but were still believed to be holding one of his brothers. The president, the son of Japanese immigrants, apparently had planned to attend the party but was delayed on a trip to the provinces.
The captives also include Peru's foreign minister, agriculture minister, supreme court president and the current and past chiefs of the anti-terrorism police.

In Quito, Ecuadoran President Abdala Bucaram offered asylum to the rebels. "We have stated clearly that if we can be of help, providing the Peruvian government asks for it, we would accede to that," Bucaram said when asked by journalists if Ecuador would give asylum to the guerrillas.
Attempts by the MRTA and the previously better-known Shining Path to overthrow the government have cost 30,000 lives and $25 billion in infrastructure damage since 1980.
